result.markdown: --- title: "Session 2 — Checking Assumptions" subtitle: "Independence · what must be normal · plots before tests · normality tests and their traps · equal variances · when assumptions fail · Lab 2" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: the design chooses the **family** of test - Today: the **assumptions** that decide between a parametric test (t, ANOVA, Pearson) and its rank-based partner - By the end you can: - say **what exactly** has to be normal for each test - read a histogram and a **Q-Q plot** - use normality tests **without being fooled** by them - check equal spread, and know why **Welch** is the safe default - choose what to do when an assumption fails, and **report it** ::: ## Three assumptions behind most tests | Assumption | What it means | How you check it | |---|---|---| | **Independence** | one person's value tells you nothing about another's | **the design** (no test can check it) | | **Shape** | the right thing is roughly **normal** | plots first, then tests | | **Equal spread** | groups have similar variances | compare SDs, Levene; or use **Welch** | ::: {.key} Categorical tests have their own assumption (enough **expected** counts): Session 3. ::: # Topic 1 — Independence {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Independence comes from the design ::: {.incremental} - **Broken** when the same person is measured twice (before and after, 0, 3 and 6 months) → use a **paired** or **repeated-measures** test - **Broken** when people come in clusters (families, villages, wards) → Advanced track, workshop A4 - **Not broken** by people being similar: two women of the same age are still independent observations ::: ::: {.warn} A test for independent groups on paired data gives the **wrong** p-value. Session 4 shows how wrong. ::: # Topic 2 — Normality {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## What has to be normal? | Test | What should be roughly normal | |---|---| | One-sample t | the values themselves | | Independent t, one-way ANOVA | the values **within each group** (the residuals) | | **Paired t** | the **differences** (after − before), **not** each column | | Repeated-measures ANOVA | the residuals at each time point | | Pearson correlation | the pairs, and the relationship must be **linear** | ::: {.key} Testing the whole outcome column when the test compares groups or pairs checks the wrong thing. ::: ## Look first: the Q-Q plot ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s2_assumptions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: - **Points on the line**: roughly normal (height, skewness -0.02) - **Points curving away at one end**: a long tail (glucose, skewness 4.4) ## Three normality tests | Test | Good at | Watch out | |---|---|---| | **Shapiro–Wilk** `shapiro.test()` | most powerful all-round; n from 3 to 5,000 | very large n: flags trivial departures | | **Kolmogorov–Smirnov** `ks.test()` | comparing with a **fully specified** distribution | needs the mean and SD *given in advance*; weak in the tails | | **Lilliefors** `nortest::lillie.test()` | KS when mean and SD are **estimated** from the data | the version to use instead of plain KS | | **Anderson–Darling** `nortest::ad.test()` | more sensitive in the **tails** | same large-n problem | ::: {.key} All of them answer one question: "could these data come from a normal distribution?" None says whether the departure **matters** for your test. ::: ## Trap 1: KS against the wrong normal ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ks.test(p$height, "pnorm")$p.value # compares with mean 0, SD 1! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ks.test(p$height, "pnorm", mean(p$height), sd(p$height))$p.value # mean and SD from the data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9198377 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lillie.test(p$height)$p.value # the correct version ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6463462 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} `ks.test(x, "pnorm")` asks whether height looks like a **standard** normal (mean 0, SD 1). It always says no, for any real measurement. With the mean and SD estimated from the data, use **Lilliefors**: height is compatible with normal (p = 0.646). ::: ## Trap 2: the answer depends on n ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **All 631 adults**, Shapiro–Wilk: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |variable | skewness| p| |:--------|--------:|---------:| |height | -0.02| p = 0.778| |weight | -0.02| p = 0.580| |age | 0.40| p < 0.001| |glucose | 4.37| p < 0.001| ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **50 random adults**, age, three draws: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | draw | Shapiro-Wilk| |:----:|------------:| | 1 | p = 0.004| | 2 | p = 0.345| | 3 | p = 0.034| ::: ::: ::: ::: - Large n: a mild skew in age (0.40) is "significant", yet a t-test on 631 ages is fine - Small n: the verdict changes with the luck of the draw. **Never test a random subsample** ## Why mild skew rarely matters ::: {.incremental} - t-tests and ANOVA compare **means**, and means of large samples are close to normal even when the data are not (**central limit theorem**) - Rough guide: with **30 or more per group** and no extreme outliers, mild skew (|skewness| < 1) does little harm - What does matter: **heavy tails and outliers** (glucose up to 487 mg/dL), **small groups**, and **very unequal** group sizes with unequal spread ::: ::: {.key} Decide with the **plot**, the **skewness**, the **sample size** and the **question**. A normality test is one input, not the judge. ::: # Topic 3 — Equal spread {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Compare the spreads ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> group_by(sex_of_participants) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight), sd = sd(weight)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 sex_of_participants n mean sd 1 female 349 70.0 15.6 2 male 282 69.3 15.1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} leveneTest(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median) Df F value Pr(>F) group 1 0.0453 0.8316 629 ``` ::: ::: - **Levene** (`car::leveneTest`, centred on the median) is robust to non-normal data; **Bartlett** is not - Rough guide: the larger SD under **twice** the smaller is rarely a problem with similar group sizes ## Welch is the safe default ::: {.incremental} - `t.test()` in R runs **Welch's t-test** unless you add `var.equal = TRUE` - Equal variances: Welch and Student give almost the **same** answer (weight by sex: p = 0.539 vs 0.540) - Unequal variances, unequal group sizes: Student's t can be badly wrong; Welch stays correct - **Testing variances first and then choosing** the test adds its own errors ::: ::: {.key} Use **Welch** for two groups and **Welch ANOVA** (`oneway.test()`) for several. Report Levene only if a reviewer asks. ::: # Topic 4 — When an assumption fails {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Four honest options | Problem | First | Then | |---|---|---| | Impossible values | check the **source**; correct or exclude, and report | sensitivity analysis | | Skewed, positive data | **log transform**, then a t-test on the log scale (ratio of geometric means) | check the plot again | | Skew or outliers that stay | **rank-based** test (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis) | report medians (IQR) | | Unequal spread | **Welch** t or Welch ANOVA | — | | Paired or clustered data | a **paired** or **repeated-measures** test | Advanced track (A4) for clusters | ## Write what you did ::: {.eq} "Distributions were inspected with histograms and Q-Q plots. Height and weight were approximately normal and are summarised as mean (SD); age and glucose were right-skewed and are summarised as median (IQR). Groups were compared with Welch's t-test or, for skewed variables, the Mann–Whitney U test." ::: - Name the **method of checking**, the **decision**, and the **test used** - No need to print every normality p-value ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 2 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `stats-workshop/labs/lab2_assumptions.R` - histograms and Q-Q plots for four variables - Shapiro–Wilk, Lilliefors and Anderson–Darling, and the KS trap - normality of the **differences** for a paired comparison - Levene's test, and Welch vs Student - a log transform, and when it is not enough ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t2q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dps14r.45gb3f" data-show="VGhlIDYtbW9udGggbWludXMgcHJlc2VudGF0aW9uIGRpZmZlcmVuY2VzIHBlciBwZXJzb24=" data-explain="QSBwYWlyZWQgdC10ZXN0IGlzIGEgb25lLXNhbXBsZSB0LXRlc3Qgb24gdGhlIGRpZmZlcmVu Y2VzLCBzbyBvbmx5IHRoZSBkaWZmZXJlbmNlcyBuZWVkIHRvIGJlIHJvdWdobHkgbm9ybWFs LiBUaGUgdHdvIGNvbHVtbnMgY2FuIGVhY2ggYmUgc2tld2VkLg=="} For a paired t-test of fasting glucose at presentation and at 6 months, what should be roughly normal? - Fasting glucose at presentation, tested on its own - Both glucose columns, each one tested separately on its own - The pooled glucose values from both visits together - The 6-month minus presentation differences per person ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t2q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dpsedd.45gpkp" data-show="SXQgY29tcGFyZXMgaGVpZ2h0IHdpdGggYSBub3JtYWwgb2YgbWVhbiAwIGFuZCBTRCAx" data-explain="V2l0aG91dCBhIG1lYW4gYW5kIFNELCBrcy50ZXN0KCkgdXNlcyB0aGUgc3RhbmRhcmQgbm9y bWFsIChtZWFuIDAsIFNEIDEpLCB3aGljaCBubyBoZWlnaHQgY2FuIG1hdGNoLiBXaXRoIHBh cmFtZXRlcnMgZXN0aW1hdGVkIGZyb20gdGhlIGRhdGEsIHVzZSB0aGUgTGlsbGllZm9ycyB0 ZXN0Lg=="} ks.test(p$height, "pnorm") gives p < 0.001 although height looks normal on a Q-Q plot. Why? - It compares height with a normal of mean 0 and SD 1 - Height is not normal; the Q-Q plot hides its skew - The KS test cannot be used for continuous variables - The sample of 631 is too small for a KS test to work ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t2q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dpsrm3.45h423" data-show="QSB0LXRlc3QgaXMgcmVhc29uYWJsZTogbWlsZCBza2V3IGFuZCBsYXJnZSBncm91cHM=" data-explain="SW4gbGFyZ2Ugc2FtcGxlcyBub3JtYWxpdHkgdGVzdHMgZmxhZyBzbWFsbCBkZXBhcnR1cmVz LiBXaXRoIG1pbGQgc2tldyBhbmQgbGFyZ2UgZ3JvdXBzIHRoZSBtZWFuIGlzIHdlbGwgYmVo YXZlZCAoY2VudHJhbCBsaW1pdCB0aGVvcmVtKSwgc28gYSB0LXRlc3QgaXMgZmluZS4gUmVt b3ZpbmcgZGF0YSBvciBzdWJzYW1wbGluZyB0byBjaGFuZ2UgYSBwLXZhbHVlIGlzIG5vdC4="} With 631 adults, Shapiro-Wilk gives p < 0.001 for age (skewness 0.4). What follows for a t-test comparing mean age? - A t-test cannot be used; switch to a rank-based test - A t-test is reasonable: mild skew and large groups - Remove the oldest adults until the test is not significant - Test 50 random adults instead to get a fairer p-value ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t2q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dpt4us.45hijg" data-show="SXQgc3RheXMgY29ycmVjdCB3aGVuIHZhcmlhbmNlcyBkaWZmZXIgYW5kIGxvc2VzIGxpdHRs ZSB3aGVuIGVxdWFs" data-explain="V2VsY2gncyB0ZXN0IGRvZXMgbm90IGFzc3VtZSBlcXVhbCB2YXJpYW5jZXMuIFdoZW4gdGhl eSBhcmUgZXF1YWwgaXQgYWdyZWVzIGNsb3NlbHkgd2l0aCBTdHVkZW50J3MgdDsgd2hlbiB0 aGV5IGFyZSBub3QsIGl0IGtlZXBzIHRoZSBlcnJvciByYXRlIHJpZ2h0Lg=="} Why is Welch's t-test a good default for comparing two independent means? - It does not need the values within each group to be numeric at all - It stays correct when variances differ and loses little when equal - It usually gives smaller p-values than Student's t for the same data - It removes the need to check the data for impossible measurements ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t2q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="dpti3i.45hx0u" data-show="VGhhdCBlYWNoIG9ic2VydmF0aW9uIGlzIGluZGVwZW5kZW50IG9mIHRoZSBvdGhlcnM=" data-explain="SW5kZXBlbmRlbmNlIGRlcGVuZHMgb24gaG93IHRoZSBkYXRhIHdlcmUgY29sbGVjdGVkOiBy ZXBlYXRlZCBtZWFzdXJlbWVudHMgb24gdGhlIHNhbWUgcGVvcGxlLCBvciBjbHVzdGVycyBz dWNoIGFzIGZhbWlsaWVzIGFuZCB2aWxsYWdlcy4gTm8gdGVzdCBvbiB0aGUgZGF0YSBjYW4g Y29uZmlybSBpdC4="} Which assumption can only be judged from the study design, not tested on the data? - That the outcome is roughly normal within each group - That the groups have roughly equal variances - That each observation is independent of the others - That no expected count in the table is below five ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Know **what** must be normal: residuals, **differences**, not the raw column - **Plot first** (histogram, Q-Q); tests support the plot, and their verdict depends on n - `ks.test(x, "pnorm")` is a trap: use **Lilliefors** - **Welch** by default; rank-based tests or a log scale when skew or outliers stay - Report **how** you checked and **what** you decided ::: **Next:** Session 3: categorical outcomes

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
